rv.q: This economically delivered production by Lindsay Posner keeps you gripped, although Ryan Craig’s adaptation flattens the book’s depth and speaks rather too prosaically, even daring to change the plot to circumvent some of the complexities of its staging.
The play certainly absorbs and even entertains the audience, as we watch the protagonist Winston Smith, a lover of literature, being lured into the trap set by O'Brien played by Keith Allen.
It’s a faithful retelling of the story that will play well for those looking for a solid dramatisation, without reaching its theatrical potency.
Anniversary staging of George Orwell’s classic is visually striking, but emotionally unengaging
This may be the most disturbing but educative play you can currently see, but everyone should be urged to take the opportunity while they still legally can.
1984 is a powerful, thought-provoking, albeit slightly disturbing and traumatising show that’ll stay with you and make you think about what it would be like to live in a world like this.
Posner’s production is good, rather than doubleplusgood (as Newspeak would have it), and worth catching on its brief tour .

cn.t: A solid but unspectacular adaptation that effectively conveys Orwell's dystopian nightmare and state control, though it struggles to escape comparisons to the acclaimed Icke/McMillan version and suffers from a lackluster central romance.
